title: Linked Lists

steps.title: Understand a node
steps.content: A linked list is made of nodes. A singly linked-list node stores data and a pointer/reference to the next node. The head points to the first node; the last node points to null.
steps.example: 10 → 20 → 30 → null. The head points to the node containing 10.

steps.title: Recognize the tail
steps.prompt: In 5 → 8 → 12 → null, what does the next pointer of the node containing 12 hold?
steps.explanation: The final node has no successor, so its next pointer is null.

steps.title: Insert at the head
steps.content: To insert a new node at the head, set newNode.next = head, then update head = newNode. Both pointer updates are important.
steps.example: Before: 10 → 20. Insert 5: set 5.next=10, then head=5, giving 5 → 10 → 20.
steps.tip: Set the new node's next pointer before replacing the head reference.

steps.title: Know the trade-off
steps.prompt: What is the time complexity of accessing the kth element of a singly linked list from its head?
steps.explanation: You must follow next pointers from the head until reaching the kth node, so access is O(n).

steps.title: Singly versus doubly linked
steps.content: A singly linked list points forward. A doubly linked list stores both next and previous pointers, enabling backward traversal at the cost of extra memory and pointer maintenance.

questions.prompt: What does the head of a linked list reference?
questions.explanation: The head is the reference to the first node.

questions.prompt: What marks the end of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: The tail node's next pointer is null.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the head when the head pointer is available?
questions.explanation: Only a constant number of pointer assignments are needed.

questions.prompt: Which structure supports forward and backward traversal?
questions.explanation: A doubly linked list has both next and previous pointers.

questions.prompt: Why is random indexing slower in a linked list than in an array?
options: Nodes are reached by following pointers
questions.explanation: A linked list does not provide direct index-based memory access.

learning_objectives: Trace traversal from the head pointer.
Compare linked-list access with array access.
Understand insertion and deletion pointer changes.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A linked list supports O(1) indexing.
common_misconceptions.correction: Finding the kth node requires traversal and takes O(n).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Deleting a node always needs shifting.
common_misconceptions.correction: A singly linked list can unlink a node by changing a previous node's next pointer.

common_misconceptions.misconception: The head pointer is the entire list.
common_misconceptions.correction: The head points to the first node; each node links to the next node.
